title: Chess: What Are the Pieces Worth?
subject: thinking

sections.body: Players give each piece a number to help them decide whether a trade is good. These are guides, not rules. A pawn is worth 1, a knight 3, a bishop 3, a rook 5 and a queen 9. The king cannot be traded, because losing it ends the game.
Count the points when you trade. If you capture a rook (5) and lose a knight (3), you gain 2 points. That is a good trade. If you give up a queen (9) for a rook (5), you lose 4 points.
The numbers are only a guide. Checkmate beats everything: a player who can give checkmate does not mind losing a queen. Sometimes position matters more than points.
Write down the point value of everything you captured and everything you lost in your last game. Who was ahead?
Point values help beginners avoid giving away pieces. Ask your child to count before every capture: 'what do I win, and what might I lose?'.

quiz.q: Which piece is worth more, a rook or a bishop?
hints: Think about how many points each piece is worth.
A bishop is worth about 3. What is a rook worth?
Example: a knight is worth 3 and a queen is worth 9, so the queen is worth more. Compare the rook and the bishop in the same way.
quiz.explain: A rook is worth about 5 points and a bishop about 3.

quiz.q: About how many pawns is a queen worth?
hints: Look at the queen's point value in the lesson.
Example: a rook is worth 5 points, so it is worth 5 pawns. Use the queen's value instead.
quiz.explain: A queen is worth about 9 points, which is about 9 pawns.

quiz.q: You capture a rook (5) and then lose your knight (3) in return. What is the result in points?
hints: Add up what you won, then take away what you lost.
Example: winning a bishop (3) and losing a pawn (1) gives 3 - 1 = 2 points gained. Do the same with 5 and 3.
quiz.explain: You won 5 points and lost 3, so you are 2 points ahead.
